deep.reconstruction:
This page has no computations. It is a draft of the opening of Section 20 of Riemann's Göttingen doctoral dissertation, 'Grundlagen für eine allgemeine Theorie der Functionen einer veränderlichen complexen Grösse' (1851). The printed text of Section 20 is almost word for word the same, with small changes such as printed 'ausgedrückter' where the draft has 'bedingter'.

Content, restated:

(1) Why complex quantities were introduced. They came from the theory of simple dependence laws between variables that are given by 'Größenoperationen'. Footnote 1 lists these operations: addition/subtraction, multiplication/division, integration/differentiation. A dependence law is simpler the fewer operations it needs. Riemann claims that finitely many such operations define every function used in analysis so far. Letting the variables take complex values brings out a 'harmony and regularity' that otherwise stays hidden.

(2) The cases treated so far nearly all reduce to two kinds of dependence between two variables w and z:
- (a) w is algebraic in z, i.e. F(z,w)=0 with F a polynomial (footnote 2);
- (b) dw/dz is an algebraic function of z, i.e. w is an abelian integral ∫R(z,s)dz with s algebraic over z.
Historical examples: algebraic functions, circular functions (e.g. arcsin z = ∫dz/sqrt(1-z^2), whose derivative is algebraic), elliptic and abelian functions.

(3) A crossed-out paragraph (one diagonal stroke), rewritten in the right column. Earlier methods took an explicit expression as the definition of a function. That expression gives the value for every argument. Proving two expressions equal therefore meant transforming one into the other, i.e. checking agreement at every point. Riemann's investigation shows that, because of the general character of a function of a complex variable, part of the data in such a definition follows from the rest. The data are reduced to what is necessary, so it is enough to check agreement on a much smaller set.

In modern terms this is uniqueness for holomorphic functions:
- the identity theorem (agreement on a set with an accumulation point);
- more specifically Riemann's own principle from earlier sections: a function is determined by its boundary and discontinuity conditions on a Riemann surface (Dirichlet-principle uniqueness).

(4) The programme. A theory built on these foundations would fix the 'Gestaltung' of the function (its values everywhere) without any expression, by adding to the general concept of a complex function only the necessary distinguishing features (Merkmale). Only afterwards would it pass to particular expressions. On the next page these features are boundary and discontinuity conditions. Example given there: single-valued on a finite-sheeted cover of the sphere, with only poles of finite order, implies algebraic.

The page proves nothing. It is methodological and historical framing. The step from (3) to (4), that intrinsic properties determine the function, is my paraphrase of what the next page makes explicit.
errors: No mathematical errors: there are no calculations on the page.

Footnote 1 says finitely many of the listed operations define all functions used in analysis up to then. This is a heuristic claim and not strictly accurate unless 'integration' is read broadly (limits, infinite series and products are not listed). Riemann explicitly leaves the related question open: whether 'complex function' coincides with 'dependence expressible by operations'.

The claim that agreement 'in a much smaller range' suffices is stated without proof here. It rests on results from earlier sections of the dissertation (Dirichlet-principle uniqueness) and on the identity theorem. As Weierstrass later stressed, the Dirichlet principle step was not rigorous at the time.

results.what: Classifies the known classical cases as algebraic functions (algebraic relation F(z,w)=0) and functions with algebraic derivative (abelian integrals). This covers circular, elliptic and abelian functions.
results.modern_name: Algebraic functions and abelian integrals on algebraic curves
results.usually_credited_to: Abel, Jacobi, Euler (historical background); framing by Riemann 1851/1857

results.what: A complex function is determined by fewer data than its values everywhere: two expressions agree everywhere once they agree on a much smaller set or under the necessary conditions.
results.modern_name: Identity theorem / uniqueness of analytic continuation; determination by boundary and singularity data
results.usually_credited_to: Cauchy, Riemann (1851 dissertation); identity theorem in Weierstrass's form

results.what: Programme of defining functions by intrinsic properties (the 'Gestaltung' plus necessary distinguishing features) rather than by formulas, with formulas seen only as ways of computing values.
results.modern_name: Riemann's conceptual/intrinsic approach to function theory (characterisation by singularities on a Riemann surface)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a working draft of Section 20 of Riemann's published 1851 dissertation and closely matches the printed text. The only extra interest is philological: the deleted paragraph and wording variants such as 'bedingter' for printed 'ausgedrückter'.

checkable.asserts: The circular function arcsin has an algebraic derivative, so it belongs to class (b), functions whose differential quotient is algebraic.
arctan also has an algebraic (rational) derivative.
The incomplete elliptic integral of the first kind, as a function of z = sin(phi), has an algebraic derivative (class (b)).
Illustrates the identity principle: a relation proved for real arguments holds for all complex z, since both sides are entire.
w = sqrt(z) satisfies the algebraic equation w**2 - z = 0, so it is an algebraic function in the sense of footnote 2.

transcription_corrections: Line 2: the image reads 'durch Größenoperationen bedingter'; the printed dissertation has 'ausgedrückter'. The deleted word at the start of line 3 appears to be 'einfacher' (struck through) before 'Abhängigkeitsgesetze', as transcribed.

The large left-column paragraph 'Die bisherigen Methoden ... im Allgemei-' is cancelled by a single diagonal stroke, not by line-by-line strikes; its replacement is the right-column text beginning 'Die bisherigen Methoden, diese Functionen zu behandeln, legten stets als Definition ...'.
In the cancelled paragraph, 'ist der Schluß[?]' more plausibly reads 'ist das Geschäft' or similar; the reading is uncertain from the image.
In the right-column replacement, 'Ausdruck' and 'jeden' appear underlined in the image ('einen Ausdruck der Function', 'für jeden Werth').
